artworks.title: Aether Battling a Lion-Headed Giant (Pergamon Altar, south frieze)
artworks.description: On the south frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon, now in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin, the primordial god of the bright upper air strides into the Gigantomachy against a lion-headed Giant. The Hellenistic workshop gives Aether a winged, sky-borne energy — the luminous aithēr itself turned warrior — in one of the few monumental images that isolate him from the broader cosmogony.

artworks.title: Aether in the Gigantomachy (Pergamon Altar)
artworks.description: A closer view of the Aether group on the Pergamon Altar's Gigantomachy frieze: the deity of the clear sky grapples amid the swirling combat of gods and Giants. The relief is among the principal ancient monuments to name Aether as a fighting presence rather than a mere cosmogonic abstraction.

artworks.title: Aether against the Giants (Pergamon Altar, detail)
artworks.description: Another angle on the same south-frieze combat in Berlin: Aether's body twists above the fallen Giant as the marble still carries the drama of Hellenistic baroque. For a figure rarely given a cult image of his own, the Pergamon frieze remains the canonical ancient portrait of the upper air at war.

artworks.title: Leon and Aether (or Astraeus?) on the Pergamon Altar
artworks.description: A widely published photograph of the south frieze pairing: the lion-headed Giant Leon locked with the sky-god usually identified as Aether (some scholars prefer Astraeus). The ambiguity itself is part of the reception — a luminous celestial fighter on the most ambitious Gigantomachy that survives.
